response.executive_summary:
This report covers assessment asm-001 of Husky AI, a machine-learning image classification service. Two documents were supplied and reviewed: security-notes.md and system-overview.md. No raw source excerpts are restated here; the rendered sections and evidence appendix carry the citations.

The assessment produced four approved findings: one of high severity (fnd-005, execution of attacker code inside the production web server when a tampered serialized model is loaded) and three of medium severity (fnd-001, an unverified substituted model artifact served from the production model blob; fnd-006, injected source code or configuration packaged and delivered into production; and fnd-007, alteration or deletion of Bastion access logs by an actor holding the production access those logs record). Each of the four is recorded as a requirement that is partially satisfied for the threat it addresses, and each carries the same shape of recommendation: establish whether the requirement is met for that threat and record the control that meets it.

Seven controls were confirmed by the evidence: Bastion SSH access logging; access control on the Jupyter Notebook environment, restricted to the experimental VPC; transport encryption on the public API and the image collection path; retention of uploaded images in memory only in the Redis cache; TLS with server certificate validation on the Azure Cognitive Services image collection path; the Jupyter Notebook environment being authenticated and confined to the experimental VPC; and per-environment access control and authorization on the source code and configuration storage.

No documentation gaps were approved. Nineteen questions remain open, three of them high priority: how access is controlled to the API key storage, the authorized keys storage, and the Bastion logs storage (qst-002); whether end users are authenticated when submitting images to the public classification API or that endpoint is anonymous (qst-003); and whether the packaged model artifact is integrity-verified between being written in the experimental environment and being loaded by the production web server (qst-004). The remaining open questions concern internal transport protection, encryption at rest and key management, Redis authentication, retention and eviction, third-party image collection transport, Bastion network exposure, upload validation, default authorization posture, logging beyond the Bastion, data classification of user images, service authentication to the model storage account, log immutability, the web server dependency manifest, endpoint rate and size limits, network reachability of the web server and model blob, and API key provisioning, rotation, and scope. These are matters that could not be determined from the supplied documentation; they are not statements that the corresponding controls are absent. Three limitations attach to the findings and are set out at the end of this report.
response.system_overview:
Husky AI, as described by the approved system context, is a public image classification service built around a trained convolutional neural network, with a separate experimental environment in which images are gathered and the model is trained.

On the production side, an API Gateway (cmp-001) receives classification requests and forwards them to a simple Python web server (cmp-002), which holds uploaded images in an Azure Cache for Redis instance (cmp-013) while awaiting classification and loads the trained model from the machine learning model blob (cmp-010). A Bastion server (cmp-003) provides administrative access into production: it authenticates SSH sessions against the authorized keys storage (cmp-011), writes access and session records to the Bastion logs storage (cmp-012), and reaches the API Gateway, the Python web server, and the model blob.

On the experimental side, a Gather Images application (cmp-004) collects images from Azure Cognitive Services (cmp-014) and from third-party image tools (cmp-015), reading credentials from the API key storage (cmp-008) and writing collected images into the training and validation images blob (cmp-007). A Jupyter Notebook environment (cmp-005) reads those training and validation images and writes the serialized model to the model storage blob. A deployment service (cmp-006) reads the trained model for packaging and reads the source code and configuration storage (cmp-009), and delivers releases into production through the Bastion.

The actors in the approved context are end users (act-001), data engineers (act-002), Azure platform engineers (act-003), and the external suppliers of images — Azure Cognitive Services and third-party tools (act-004). The assets are the trained convolutional neural network model (ast-001), the training and validation images (ast-002), the API keys for external image services (ast-003), the source code and configuration (ast-004), the SSH authorized keys (ast-005), the Bastion SSH access and activity logs (ast-006), user-uploaded images awaiting classification (ast-007), and the availability of the public classification service itself (ast-008).

Three trust boundaries were approved: the public internet to production boundary (tb-001), the public internet to experimental boundary (tb-002), and the production to experimental boundary (tb-003). The last of these is the one that the model artifact, the packaged source and configuration, and the release delivery path all cross.
response.risk_summary:
The four approved findings concentrate on a single theme: the integrity of artifacts that move from the lower-trust experimental environment into the production serving path, and the ability to detect it afterwards if that movement is abused.

Three of the four findings sit on that path. fnd-001 (medium) concerns a substituted or altered model artifact written into the production model blob and served without documented verification, which the approved impact describes as destroying the integrity of the trained model (ast-001) and putting the classification behaviour of the public service (ast-008) under the actor's control, with chosen inputs receiving chosen labels. fnd-005 (high), the most severe finding in the set, extends the same write into code execution inside the production web server when a tampered serialized model is loaded, giving the actor the server's access to the model artifact, to user-uploaded images held in the cache (ast-007), and the ability to stop or corrupt the serving path. fnd-006 (medium) reaches the same destination by a different route: injected code or configuration in the source storage that is packaged and delivered into production, affecting the integrity of the packaged source and configuration (ast-004) and, through it, how uploaded images are handled, how the model is loaded, and whether the service functions at all.

The fourth finding, fnd-007 (medium), concerns detection rather than the initial compromise: Bastion access logs altered or deleted by an actor holding the production access those logs record, costing the ability to attribute or reconstruct administrative actions in production — including tampering with the model artifact, which the approved impact notes would otherwise be visible only through this record.

All four findings are recorded as partially satisfied requirements — two against the CI/CD requirement req-CICD-001, one against the administrative access requirement req-ADMIN-001, and one against the logging requirement req-LOG-002 — and each carries a recommendation to establish whether the requirement is met for the threat and to record the control that meets it. This shape matters for the reader: the approved conclusions are that a weakness is supported by evidence and that the satisfying control is not on record, not that a control has been observed to be missing.

Several confirmed controls bound the picture without closing it. Transport encryption is confirmed for the public API and the Azure Cognitive Services image collection path, but the documentation does not extend that statement to the internal flows on these findings' paths. The Jupyter Notebook environment is confirmed as authenticated and confined to the experimental VPC, though the authorization model and its holders are not described and no configuration artifact is cited. Per-environment access control on the source code and configuration storage is confirmed, but it does not distinguish read from write, nor restrict which experimental principals may modify content that will be packaged into production. Bastion SSH access logging is confirmed for all attempts, successful or not. Uploaded images are held in memory only in the Redis cache, which bounds what an actor with execution inside the production web server can recover to images resident at that time.

The open questions bear directly on this concentration. Whether the packaged model artifact is integrity-verified between the experimental write and the production load (qst-004) is the single question most likely to change the reading of fnd-001 and fnd-005. Access control on the API key, authorized keys, and Bastion logs stores (qst-002) bears on fnd-007 and on the confidentiality of external credentials, and access and immutability configuration for the Bastion logs storage (qst-017) bears on the same finding. Whether the public classification endpoint is authenticated or anonymous (qst-003), whether internal production flows are authenticated and encrypted (qst-005), and how the deployment service and notebook environment authenticate to the model storage account (qst-016) remain undetermined. No documentation gaps were approved; the undetermined matters in this assessment are carried by the open questions.

limitations.text: Finding fnd-005 rests on a stated assumption rather than on documented fact. The assessment assumed that the public-key authentication described for movement between the production and experimental environments is the mechanism by which the deployment service authenticates through the Bastion; the documentation does not say so explicitly. If the deployment service in fact authenticates by some other mechanism, the reasoning about that step of the path would need to be revisited. Separately, the approved finding records a limitation on the scope of its own attack path: the second entry branch, in which the release is modified while it is packaged and delivered through the Bastion, is not established by the cited material, which places no actor on that flow and does not establish that the flow lacks integrity or transport protection, and the "while it is packaged" variant would imply write access to the source and configuration storage or to the deployment service that the actor is not given. The first branch — a write to the model blob (cmp-010) along a documented write path — is supported and stands.

Finding fnd-006 rests on a stated assumption rather than on documented fact. The assessment took the public-key authentication described for movement between the production and experimental environments to be the mechanism by which the deployment service authenticates to the Bastion, on the basis that release delivery is described over that same path; the documentation does not state this outright. The approved finding also records that its entry condition is presented as more settled than the material supports: the precondition that write access to the source storage is available to experimental principals, and the corresponding first step of the attack path, go beyond what is documented. What is documented is that access control and authorization are configured on the Azure Blob accounts including the source and configuration storage and that access is granted per environment — the same statement that confirmed control ctl-012 records, which names no principals and does not distinguish read from write, nor restrict which experimental principals may modify content that will be packaged into production. The material establishing that the public-to-experimental boundary is password-authenticated does not establish that crossing it confers write access to that storage account.

Finding fnd-007 rests on a stated assumption rather than on documented fact. The assessment assumed that the "activity logs" named in the store inventory are SSH session records rather than per-object records of writes to the model blob; the documentation does not state which, and the finding's impact should be read with that ambiguity in mind. The approved finding also records that one step of its attack path is not carried by the cited material: removing or modifying the corresponding entries in the Bastion logs storage (cmp-012) requires the acting principal to hold modify or delete permission on that store, and that capability appears in neither the preconditions nor the cited passages. The documented onward reach of the Bastion is enumerated as the API Gateway, the web server, and the model blob; the log store is not in that list. What is established is that the Bastion itself writes session and access records to a dedicated log store as part of authentication, together with co-location of principals and store and undetermined access control on the store — none of which yields operator-level modify or delete. Open questions qst-002 and qst-017, on access control and immutability configuration for that store, remain unanswered.
